title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure (IaC), model-serving, observability, and performance. It also includes two canonical ADRs that have shaped platform behavior. Intended audience: engineers, architects, SRE, product managers, and reviewers onboarding new services.

Goals and scope
- Provide clear, actionable standards that produce consistent, observable, and maintainable services.
- Reduce integration friction between hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Ensure service reliability and predictable cost/performance tradeoffs.
- Surface required checks for PRs, CI, and production rollout.

1) API standards
Intro: All public and internal APIs must be designed for backwards compatibility, observable operation, and easy client integration. Use OpenAPI for external HTTP APIs and protobuf/gRPC for internal high-throughput RPC where latency and binary size matter.

Design principles
- Versioning: use path-based semantic versioning: /v1/, /v2/. Backwards-incompatible changes require a new major version.
- Idempotency: POSTs that change state must accept an idempotency key header X-Idempotency-Key (UUID).
- Error model: return structured errors with keys: code (machine), message (user), details (optional). Use standard HTTP status codes: 400 for client validation, 401/403 for auth, 404 for missing resources, 429 for rate limits, 500/502/503 for server faults.
- Schema & validation: publish OpenAPI schema in the API catalog. All request bodies validated in the API gateway layer; validation failures return 422 with field-level error details.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination preferred for large lists. Include next_cursor and has_more in responses.
- Rate limiting & quotas: defined per route in product docs; API gateway enforces 429 and provides Retry-After.
- Streaming: use server-sent events (SSE) or HTTP chunked-transfer for streamed generations; include sequence numbers in chunks for client reconciliation.

Security and compliance
- All external APIs require TLS 1.2+ and mTLS for Private deployments where configured.
- Sensitive fields must be redacted in logs and traces; schema annotations must include sensitive:true.
- Authentication: bearer tokens with short lived sessions; rotate keys per KMS policy.

2) Coding standards and repo hygiene
- Language-level conventions: follow established style guides (Python: PEP8 with Black, Type hints; Go: gofmt and effective go; TypeScript: eslint + prettier).
- Static checks: every repo must run linters, type checks, and security scanners in CI. PRs must pass these checks before merge.
- Tests: unit tests + integration tests required. Aim for a minimum of 60% coverage on critical runtime code; 80% for core-serving components.
- Code review: at least one reviewer from the owning team and one cross-team reviewer for infra/SDK changes. Use PR templates that include backwards-compatibility and rollout impact.
- Dependency management: pin direct dependencies in manifests. Use Dependabot or equivalent to keep dependencies up to date.

3) Infrastructure and IaC standards
- Terraform modules: canonical modules in infra/terraform-modules. Modules must be idempotent, documented, and have example usages.
- Naming conventions: resource names should follow: rdw-{service}-{env}-{resource}. Example: rdw-ingestor-prod-queue.
- Tagging: all cloud resources must include tags: team, service, environment, cost_center, compliance (if applicable).
- Secrets: do not store secrets in Git. Use KMS/Secret Manager integrations. Secrets references in configs must be via provider-specific secret URIs.
- Environments: three logical environments: staging (pre-prod), prod, and dedicated-customer. Only non-destructive migrations allowed on prod without scheduled maintenance window.
- CI/CD: gated deployments with automated smoke tests. Canary deployments enabled by default (see rollout section).

4) Model-serving standards
- Model packaging: models should be versioned using semantic tags: model-name@vYYYYMMDD-build. Artifacts stored in model registry with provenance (checksum, training dataset id, config).
- Serving interface: serve models through a stable inference API layer (same API surface across hosted, dedicated, and private). The runtime abstracts model IO so callers never rely on backend vendor specifics.
- Quantization & profiles: maintain a quantization-profiles directory describing tested quantization modes (fp16, int8, int4) and expected quality/regression thresholds per profile. Default production profile: int8 for non-sensitive workloads unless QA gate fails.
- KV cache & caching policy: prefix-level KV cache for autoregressive workloads. Cache keys must include model-version, tokenizer-version, and prefix-hash. Cache TTL defaults: 6 hours for short-term inference reuse; configurable per route.
- Batching: automatic batching managed by the runtime. Services must declare acceptable max-latency and batch-size heuristics in config for scheduler: e.g., max_latency_ms: 100, preferred_batch_size: 8.
- Versioning & rollouts: model rollouts use canary percentages and monitoring-backed promotion. Default canary: 5% for 24 hours with automatic rollback on error budget burn or regen-quality regression.

5) Observability standards
- Metrics: use Prometheus naming conventions. Metric names should be adjectives_noun_total or latency_seconds_bucket. Required metrics for each service:
  - service_request_count_total (labels: route, method, status_code)
  - service_request_duration_seconds (histogram, labels: route, method)
  - model_token_generation_count_total (labels: model, deployment)
  - model_inflight_batches (gauge, labels: model, node)
  - cache_hit_ratio (gauge, labels: model, route)
- Tracing: All RPC boundaries must have distributed tracing with W3C Trace Context. High-cardinality attributes must be avoided. Trace sampling: 100% for errors, 1% baseline for successful requests with adjustable debug overrides.
- Logging: structured JSON logs with these fields: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, message, tags. Do not log full-prompts or sensitive PII. Logs must support redaction markers.
- Dashboards & runbooks: each service must provide a default dashboard (p95/p99 latency, error rate, throughput, cache hit rate, token cost) and a one-page runbook for initial response to alerts.

6) Performance standards and SLOs
- Global availability SLOs: 99.95% for critical inference endpoints (SLO measured as successful 2xx/streaming responses excluding throttling and planned maintenance). Error budget windows: 30 days.
- Latency targets: p95 latency < 200ms for small-gen endpoints (<=512 tokens) on hosted API; p99 < 500ms. For long-form generation (>1024 tokens) document expected tail latency and chargeable cost.
- Throughput: provide capacity targets per GPU type in the model-playbook. Example baseline: A100-80GB serving a GPT-like model at sequence length 512 should sustain ~120 tokens/sec with batch_size=8 under optimized kernels.
- Cost targets: maintain per-token median cost metrics in Redwood Console. Optimize with caching, batching, and quantization first before recommending hardware scale-up.

7) Release strategy and ADR process
- ADRs: Use ADRs to document architecture tradeoffs. ADRs must include context, alternatives, decision, consequences, and owners. Keep ADRs small and linked in related_pages.
- Rollouts: default canary -> ramp -> full. Canary metrics: error rate, latency, cost-per-token, and quality regressions measured by eval harness. Automated rollback triggers: >3x baseline error rate OR latency increase >2x OR cost-per-token increase >30% OR quality metric drop beyond threshold.

8) Operational playbooks and runbooks
- Incident triage checklist: identify scope & blast radius, service ownership, revert/rollback option, activate oncall and pager-rotations, and notify affected customers.
- Postmortems: publish within 72 hours of P0 closure with timeline, root cause, impact, and action items with owners and completion dates.

9) ADR examples included
ADR-2025-08: API format decision
- Context: Need consistent external API surface that is easy for customers and tooling while internal high-throughput services require compact wire formats.
- Decision: Use OpenAPI (JSON/HTTP/REST) for external/public APIs and Protobuf/gRPC for internal high-throughput services where binary efficiency, streaming semantics, and strong typing reduce overhead. Publish OpenAPI docs to the API catalog and generate SDKs.
- Consequences: Easier customer integration and SDK generation; additional translation layer in the gateway for gRPC->HTTP where needed. Increases operational complexity but improves performance for internal paths.

ADR-2025-11: Default quantization policy for production models
- Context: Quantization reduces memory and increases throughput at potential quality cost. Team experiments found int8 acceptable for majority of non-sensitive workloads.
- Decision: Default to int8 quantization profile for production deployments unless QA gate indicates a regression above defined thresholds in regression-triage. For customer-sensitive or high-fidelity use cases, default to fp16 or unquantized models.
- Consequences: Lower per-token cost and higher packing efficiency; requires robust eval gating and a documented rollback path.

Appendices and links
- Required repo templates: link to internal repo templates and PR checklists.
- Model quantization profiles table (documented in quantization-profiles directory): includes expected latency improvements and sample RLHF-quality checks.

Maintenance
This document is owned by the Architecture & Standards working group. Review cadence: annual or whenever a platform-changing technology is introduced (new kernel, major model format change, or major observability overhaul).
